newsitem.title: USA: Hispanic residents of Illinois town settle suit.
newsitem.headline: Hispanic residents of Illinois town settle suit.

text.p: The Chicago suburb of Addison agreed to pay millions of dollars to settle a 2-year-old federal discrimination lawsuit brought by Hispanic residents who charged their homes were being destroyed unfairly.
The village will pay up to $1.4 million for urban renewal and to compensate displaced families, and an additional $2.5 million in legal fees.

The settlement, which must be approved by the U.S. District Court judge overseeing the case, included compensation to 44 dislocated families in addition to pledges to preserve existing housing, build additional homes and apartments, construct parks and pay plaintiffs' legal fees.
The plaintiffs called it the largest settlement of any private fair housing complaint in U.S. history.

The 1995 suit charged the village improperly used a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) programme -- commonly employed by municipalities to boost development in run-down districts -- to condemn several blocks where a majority of the village's 4,000 to 5,000 Hispanic residents lived.
"Effectively displacing minorities in the name of redevelopment is an affront to legitimate programmes to remove blight," said James Burns, U.S. attorney in Chicago.

The western suburb, which has a total population of 32,000, said the settlement to be paid over seven years would not cost the taxpayers, but would be paid out of the Tax Increment Financing district revenues and insurance.

"We are pleased with Addison's cooperation in working to preserve and improve these neighbourhoods instead of destroying them," said Isabelle Katz Pinzler, acting U.S. assistant attorney general for civil rights.
